rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Angular displacement (θ), angular velocity (ω = dθ/dt), and angular acceleration (α = dω/dt) describe rotational motion. For constant angular acceleration, the kinematic equations mirror linear motion. The links v = rω and a_c = rω² connect rotational and translational quantities. rpm is converted to rad/s by multiplying by 2π/60.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt (instantaneous), ω = Δθ/t (average)
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt²
Kinematic equations (constant α): ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Axis of Rotation Constraint:** Angular quantities ($ heta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$) are defined with respect to a specific fixed axis. If the axis of rotation changes orientation, the angular velocity becomes a time-dependent vector, and simple scalar kinematics no longer apply.  ·  **Kinematic Equations Applicability:** The kinematic equations (analogs of $v = u + at$) for angular motion are strictly valid *only* for constant angular acceleration ($\alpha = ext{constant}$). For time-varying $\alpha(t)$, direct integration of $d\omega/dt$ is required.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Angular velocity points ALONG THE AXIS (right-hand rule), not tangentially — this is the most common confusion.  ·  The kinematic equations for rotation are IDENTICAL in form to linear motion — just swap the variables.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: rpm to rad/s: A wheel rotates at 180 rpm. ω = 180 × 2π/60 = 18.85 rad/s.  ·  Kinematic equation: A wheel starts from rest and accelerates at 3 rad/s². After 4 s: ω = 12 rad/s, θ = 24 rad, revolutions = 24/2π ≈ 3.82 rev.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Angular displacement and angle are the same.' ✅ Angular displacement is a vector (along the axis), while angle is a scalar. For a full revolution, angular displacement = 2π rad, but the body returns to its starting position.  ·  ❌ 'Angular velocity is always constant in circular motion.' ✅ Only in UNIFORM circular motion is ω constant. In non-uniform circular motion, ω changes and there is angular acceleration.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 problems converting between rpm, rad/s, and revolutions.  ·  Solve 5 problems using the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: rpm shortcut: multiply by 2π/60 to get rad/s — memorize this conversion factor.  ·  Revolutions shortcut: divide θ (in radians) by 2π — no conversion needed.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A wheel rotates at 240 rpm. Find its angular velocity in rad/s.  ·  A disc starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 rad/s² for 6 s. Find the final angular velocity and the number of revolutions.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: rpm to rad/s conversion is tested every year — know the factor 2π/60.  ·  Kinematic equation problems (constant α) are standard — practice all four equations.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Angular velocity (ω = dθ/dt) is the rate of change of angular displacement, with direction along the axis.  ·  The kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration mirror linear motion: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ.  ·  Linear speed and angular speed are linked by v = rω — the basis of circular motion problems.  ·  Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r = rω² is directed toward the center of the circular path.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Angular displacement is measured in radians; 2π rad = 360° = 1 revolution.  ·  Angular velocity is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule), not tangential.  ·  The kinematic equations for rotation mirror linear motion: x→θ, v→ω, a→α.  ·  v = rω links linear and angular speed — the basis of all circular motion problems.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation — its direction is given by the right-hand rule.  ·  The kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration are identical in form to those for linear motion.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A fan blade rotating at 150 rpm comes to rest in 10 s. Find the angular acceleration and the angular displacement.  ·  A particle moves in a circle of radius 3 m with angular velocity ω = 2t rad/s. Find the linear speed, tangential acceleration, and centripetal acceleration at t = 3 s.  ·  A wheel of radius 0.4 m rotates at 30 rad/s. Find the linear speed at the edge and the centripetal acceleration.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Linear-angular link problems (v = rω, a = rω²) are common — know both formulas.  ·  Number of revolutions problems: use θ/(2π), not θ in radians.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Linear-angular link: A disc of radius 0.5 m rotates at 10 rad/s. Linear speed at the edge: v = 0.5 × 10 = 5 m/s. Centripetal acceleration: a = 0.5 × 100 = 50 m/s².  ·  Deceleration: A fan at 90 rpm stops in 6 s. ω₀ = 9.42 rad/s. α = −1.57 rad/s². θ = 9.42 × 6/2 = 28.27 rad ≈ 4.5 rev.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Angular displacement ($\Delta \theta$):** the angle through which a body rotates about a fixed axis. Measured in radians (rad). 1 rad = 57.3°, 2$\pi$ rad = 360°. Angular displacement is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule): positive for anticlockwise rotation.  ·  **Angular velocity ($\omega$):** the rate of change of angular displacement: $\omega = d\theta/dt$ (instantaneous), $\omega = \Delta\theta/t$ (average). Unit: rad/s. Direction: along the axis (right-hand rule). For uniform circular motion, $\omega$ is constant.  ·  **Angular acceleration ($\alpha$):** the rate of change of angular velocity: $\alpha = d\omega/dt = d^2\theta/dt^2$. Unit: rad/s$^2$. When $\alpha$ is constant, the kinematic equations mirror linear motion.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Derivation result for Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration  ·  **Reference Frame:** Angular velocity is defined in an inertial frame. If observing from a rotating reference frame, non-inertial (fictitious) forces like centrifugal or Coriolis forces appear, which must be accounted for if analyzing dynamics in that frame.  ·  Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas: multiply by 2π/60.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'The direction of angular velocity is tangential.' ❌ The direction of angular velocity is ALONG THE AXIS of rotation (right-hand rule), not tangential. Tangential velocity is v = rω, but ω itself points along the axis.  ·  ❌ 'Angular acceleration means the body is speeding up.' ✅ Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity. If α and ω have the same sign, the body speeds up; if opposite signs, it slows down.  ·  ❌ 'The kinematic equations for rotation are different from linear motion.' ✅ They are IDENTICAL in form: just replace x with θ, v with ω, and a with α. The same problem-solving approach works.
